title: Dickie Roberts: Former Child Star
full_review:
A washed-up, one-time child celeb mounts an improbable comeback and learns the true meaning of success in the unexpectedly entertaining comedy, "Dickie Roberts: Former Child Star" (Paramount).

Directed by Sam Weisman, the film imparts a positive message about the importance of home and family, while lightheartedly lampooning Hollywood's cult of celebrity. Unfortunately, the otherwise agreeable narrative is shellacked throughout by crude, sex-related humor that disqualifies it as wholly recommendable family fare.

Funnyman David Spade stars as Dickie Roberts, a former prepubescent phenom whose hit sitcom "The Glitter Gang" had made him a TV sensation back in the 1970s. Now a 35-year-old has-been, his career prospects swing between anonymity, working as a valet-parking attendant at a posh Tinseltown watering hole, and indignity, competing in cheesy celebrity boxing matches against fellow where-is-he-now wonder Emmanuel Lewis.

Convinced his star will rise again, Dickie auditions for a plum role in a major Hollywood movie to be directed by Rob Reiner -- one which, if he lands it, could be the career coup needed to jump-start his flat-lining future. But his hopes are dashed when Reiner explains that the part demands an understanding of "growing up normal" -- a slice of life the spotlight never afforded Dickie. Undeterred, Dickie rents a suburban family, complete with parents and siblings, to find out what he missed out on.

The inanity of the premise proves that first impressions can be deceiving. The movie starts off as a kamikaze-comedy piloted by yet another "Saturday Night Live" alum looking to reinvent himself on the big screen -- doomed to go down in the flames of forced, crass humor and canned shtick -- plummeting Spade's cachet to Dickie Roberts' lows. But what unfolds, in spite of the film's lewd concessions, is a surprisingly tender story. And while Spade's nasal naughtiness takes some getting used to, he imbues a rather one-note role with an appealing blend of impish charm and vulnerability, providing viewers a sympathetic rooting interest and making the film's at times heavy-handed family-values epiphanies easy to applaud.

Buttressing Spade's adolescent antics is the film's ringing endorsement of the precedence of authentic love over the superficiality of fleeting fame. Regrettably, Weisman shows little faith in the power of his story's message or in Spade's talent, acquiescing to lowest-common-denominator interests by peppering the film with superfluous sex- and drug-related humor in an effort to elicit some cheap chuckles, including a raunchy theme involving Dickie's self-absorbed girlfriend (Alyssa Milano).

On a lighter note, "Dickie Roberts" takes some clever jabs at the movie industry and at America's fascination with celebrity, especially with those fizzled stars whose trajectories have fallen off the astronomical charts. The narrative is bookended by two sequences that capture this almost pathological obsession with lives burned by the spotlight: a faux expose documenting Dickie's early life and a riotous "We Are the World"-type closing-credit musical send-off, performed by a virtual Who's Who of prime-time dysfunction.

Yet the scene which offers viewers raised on TV dinners the best flashback bang for their buck involves Dickie playing poker with fellow "formers" Leif Garrett, Danny Bonaduce, Corey Feldman, Dustin Diamond (Screech from "Saved by the Bell") and Barry Williams (aka Greg Brady). Williams, out of poker chips, ups the ante with the infamous football that broke Marcia's nose.
Marcia, Marcia, Marcia. It's always about Marcia.

Due to recurring crude, sexually related humor, a sensual encounter, as well as some crass language and drug references, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
